WRIT PETITION [CIVIL] NO.815/2026
ADITHIAN RAJMOHAN NAIR & ORS.        Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
THE UNION OF INDIA & ORS.              Respondent(s)
 
WITH
WRIT PETITION [C] NO.810/2026
O R D E R
We have heard the learned counsel appearing for
the  writ  petitioners  and  the  learned  Solicitor
General (SG) appearing for the respondent(s).
Unfortunately, the present situation has been
brought forth in view of the prevalent war situation
in the Middle East, which is under the control of
none.
The respondent(s) have taken a policy decision,
taking into consideration the prevailing situation,
in order to mitigate the sufferings of the students.
The suggestions made by the learned counsel appearing
for the writ petitioners, have been duly considered
by the learned SG. On the last date of hearing,
learned  SG  had  come  forth  with  the  following
suggestion:
“A. The Board wishes to place on record,
unequivocally, that its foremost concern

## Page 166

2
through this entire episode has been the
welfare and academic future of the students
affected  by  circumstances  that  were
entirely  beyond  their,  and  the  Board’s
control.   The  Assessment  Scheme  dated
27.03.2026 and the subsequent policy for
private candidates dated 21.06.2026 were
both  devised  as  good-faith,
methodologically sound attempts to ensure
that no student is left without a result
merely because war-related conditions made
it impossible to hold an examination. The
Board has consistently proceeded on the
footing  that  every  affected  candidate,
whether  a  regular  school  student  or  a
private candidate such as the Petitioner,
must be treated fairly, consistently, and
without avoidable delay.
B. It is submitted that the Board remains
fully alive to the anxiety that a pending
or provisional result causes to a student
at the threshold of higher education, and
it has therefore built into its own Scheme
a further safeguard:the possibility of a
fresh examination for students dissatisfied
with the assessment made under the Scheme,
to be offered the moment conditions in the
affected countries become conducive and the
exercise becomes logistically feasible.
C. The Board reiterates before this Hon’ble
Court that it is prepared to take any and
every step reasonably necessary to secure
the  academic  future  of  the  students

## Page 167

3
affected  by  the  cancellation  of
examinations  in  the  West  Asia  region
whether by way of continued facilitation of
admissions on the basis of provisional or
assessed results, expedited re-evaluation
and verification facilities, or the conduct
of  a  special  examination  as  and  when
feasible. The submissions above regarding
the time required for a fresh examination
are placed before this Hon’ble Court so
that  any  direction  this  Hon’ble  Court
considers appropriate can be moulded with
full knowledge of the practical steps and
time  genuinely  needed  to  protect  the
interests of all 23,052 similarly situated
candidates, and not the Petitioner alone.”
Learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  writ
petitioners reiterated the earlier suggestion made on
behalf of the writ petitioners, to facilitate all of
them to write the exam along with the other students
who  are  scheduled  to  write  the  papers  in  the
compartmental exam.
As rightly submitted by the learned SG, it is
not feasible to extend the aforesaid facility to all
other students, including the writ petitioners.
On the contrary, the suggestion given by the
learned  SG,  as  recorded  in  our  order  dated
28.07.2026, is once again taken on record, regarding
compressing the time limit for the next exam from 82
days to 70 days, which shall be left to the wisdom of

## Page 168

4
the respondents to undertake.  
We are inclined to dispose of the present writ
petitions so as to enable the writ petitioners to be
in a position to compete in the next examination at
the earliest point of time, and also facilitate them
to compete for higher studies next year.
The  Writ  Petitions  stand  disposed  of,
accordingly.
Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

1. On 17.07.2026, a detailed order was passed which is
reproduced hereinbelow:
1

## Page 189

“1. Delay condoned.
2. Appellant is the successful resolution
applicant. The submission on behalf of the
appellant  is  that  under  the  Resolution
Plan,  in  paragraphs  10.9  to  10.11,
DMRC/Delhi Development Authority/MCD/ Any
Departments/Authorities were to allow the
change in management and shareholding of
the  PIPL/Corporate  Debtor  and  were  to
provide  other  required  permissions  for
continuation of the existing rights, lease,
licenses etc. to the new management on the
basis of Resolution plan approved by the
Adjudicating  Authority.  Further,  Delhi
Metro  Rail  Corporation  (“DMRC”)  was
required to revive the Concession Agreement
in  favour  of  the  Corporate  Debtor  as
assigned  by  Pratibha  Industries  Limited
(“PIL”) in favour of the Corporate Debtor
in  full  force  and  effect  without  any
additional liability towards the Corporate
Debtor/ Resolution Applicant.
3. It is the case of the appellant that the
order of the National Company Law Tribunal
(“Adjudicating Authority”) dated 30.07.2024
approved  the  Resolution  Plan.  Paragraph
10.2 of the approval order stated that the
Resolution Plan shall be binding on the
Corporate Debtor, its employees, members,
creditors,  Central  Government,  State
Government or any local authority to whom a
debt in respect of the payment of dues
arising under any law for the time being in
force  is  due,  guarantors  and  other
stakeholders  involved  in  the  Resolution
Plan, so that the revival of the Corporate
Debtor comes under force with immediate
effect.
4. It is also the case of the appellant
that the approval order dated 30.07.2024
passed  by  the  Adjudicating  Authority
approving the Resolution Plan has attained
finality  for  want  of  challenge  by  any
stakeholder and, therefore, DMRC, which is
a stakeholder, is bound by the approved
Resolution Plan.
5. The record reflects that the stand of
DMRC was that the Concession Agreement was
terminated prior to initiation of Corporate
2

## Page 190

Insolvency  Resolution  Process  (“CIRP”).
Therefore, the rights of the parties qua
the  subject  matter  of  the  Concession
Agreement stood crystallized prior to the
initiation of CIRP and those rights cannot
be affected by the Resolution Plan.
6. At this stage, the submission on behalf
of the appellant is that the Successful
Resolution Applicant on approval of the
plan steps into the shoes of the Corporate
Debtor and can take recourse to all the
remedies that would be otherwise available
to  the  Corporate  Debtor  against  the
termination of the Concession Agreement. He
further submits that already arbitration
clause stood invoked and, therefore, the
validity of termination of the Concession
Agreement would have to be determined in
terms thereof.
7. It is also the case of the appellant
that vide letter dated 24.04.2026, DMRC has
taken a stand that Concession Agreement,
under which PIL/PIPL were granted rights
for  development  of  the  project,  stood
terminated  on  01.03.2017  and  cannot  be
restored. However, in the very same letter,
it is also stated that DMRC is ready to
consider  conciliation  /  arbitration  in
accordance with law and, hence, Prime Infra
Park may invoke conciliation by submitting
a proper formal request.
8.  In  that  context,  the  submission  on
behalf  of  the  appellant  is  that  once
arbitration  clause  stands  invoked,  and
there is nothing in the resolution plan
extinguishing such proceeding, the dispute
would  have  to  be  resolved  through
arbitration/  conciliation,  but  paragraph
14(i) of the impugned order may come in the
way of resolution of the dispute as it
holds that no direction can be issued to
the  appellant  to  revive  the  Concession
Agreement terminated on 01.03.2017.
9.  In  the  above  backdrop,  we  deem  it
appropriate to require the respondents to
file their affidavit to ascertain their
stand as to whether they are willing to
undertake  the  arbitration  /conciliation
proceedings qua revival of the Concession
3

## Page 191

Agreement.
10. Issue notice, returnable on 12.08.2026.
11. Notice on behalf of the respondents has
been accepted by Mr. Tarun Johri.
12. In the meantime, the petitioner would
not be required to make deposit of any
further amount under the Resolution Plan.” 
2. Pursuant to the above order, an affidavit has been 
filed on behalf of DMRC.  In paragraph 6 thereof it is 
stated as under:
“6. Without prejudice to its legal rights
and contentions, R-1/DMRC is agreeable to
acknowledge the legal status of Appellant,
to maintain conciliation proceedings under
the CA with respect to subject matter of
issues/disputes in question.  However, such
conciliation proceedings would be subject
to exercise of all legal right available
with  R-1/DMRC  inter  alia  including
objections  qua  maintainability  of  such
conciliation proceedings, if any, raised by
R-1/SRA  in  terms  of  Dispute  Resolution
Clause provided under Article 12 (Pg.116)
of CA, which shall be governed as per
relevant  provisions  of  Arbitration  and
Conciliation Act, 1996.
However,  subject  to  conciliation
proceedings shall in no manner be treated
as a waiver on the part of R-1/DMRC to
raise  all  its  rights,  contentions  and
defences  etc.  with  regard  to
maintainability/admissibility of claims for
re-instatement/revival of CA or monetary
claim, if any, raised by Appellant before
conciliator or an Arbitral Tribunal and R-
1/DMRC hereby, reserve its rights to raise
all  its  legal  and  factual  contentions
before  an  appropriate  forum  inter  alia
including the objection qua such claims
being  barred  by  law  of  limitation  and
principles of estoppel.”
3. Dr. Singhvi, Senior Advocate, who represents the
appellant  submits  that  since  DMRC  is  agreeable  to
4

## Page 192

undertake conciliation proceedings, it would be in the
fitness of things that the matter be taken up after six
weeks and in the meantime, conciliation proceedings may
be  held  without  prejudice  to  the  rights  of  the
respective parties.
4. Mr. R.Venkataramani, Attorney General for India, who
represents the first respondent (DMRC) submits that
DMRC is willing to undertake conciliation proceedings
without prejudice to any of their rights regarding the
claim being barred by limitation.
5. In view of the above, without expressing any opinion
on the merits of the rival claims and their rights, we
deem it appropriate to direct that this matter be listed
after six weeks so that in the meantime, the parties may
undertake conciliation proceedings.
6. On the joint request of the learned counsel for the
parties, we deem it appropriate to appoint Hon’ble Mr.
Justice Abhay Manohar Sapre, a former Judge of the
Supreme Court of India as a Conciliator.  The fees of

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
The Special Leave Petitions arise from the common order of the
High Court of Telangana at Hyderabad dated 21.05.2025 in CMA No.221
of 2024 and CMA No.230 of 2024. The said orders were passed
confirming a temporary injunction granted in two IAs in O.S. No.150
of  2023  by  the  IVth  Additional  District  Judge,  Ranga  Reddy
District.
2. We refer to the parties by their status in the suit.
3. The plaintiff, is the 1st respondent in the SLP, the defendant
No.2 is the petitioner in the SLP and defendant No.3 is the 4th
respondent in the SLP. The suit was for declaration of title and
2

## Page 195

the recovery of possession of land scheduled, comprised in Survey
No.299 situated at Puppalaguda Village, Rajendranagar Mandal, Ranga
Reddy District, from the defendants 1 to 3, the 1st defendant being
one Mr. Sai Narasimha Rao. A temporary injunction was granted
restraining the defendants from altering the nature of the property
and carrying out alienation of the suit schedule property, was
challenged in two appeals before the High Court of Telangana, which
affirmed the injunction by the impugned orders.
4. In the SLP, even before notice was issued, the plaintiff and
one of the defendants-petitioner in Special Leave Petition Nos.
31518-31519 of 2025, agreed to a suggestion to resolve the disputes
through mediation recorded in order dated 05.12.2025. Respondent
No.4, who was the last purchaser of the subject property, was also
directed to join the mediation. This Court appointed Hon’ble Mr.
Justice L. Nageswara Rao, a Former Judge of the Supreme Court, to
act as a Mediator.
5. The mediation has culminated in the resolution of the disputes
between the plaintiff, M/s. A.R. Resurgence Resources LLP and
defendant Nos.2 and 3, M/s. DRS Infra and M/s ZNS Builders &
Developer Pvt. Ltd. respectively.
6. A Memorandum of Understanding cum Settlement executed on
04.05.2026 at Hyderabad, is also placed before us. We take the same
on record.
7. On the last day of hearing, intervenors appeared through
Counsel and argued that their rights would be impaired if the
settlement arrived at, without their junction, is affirmed by this
Court. The intervenors had filed impleading petitions in the suit.
3

## Page 196

We hence directed the Registry of the High Court of Telangana to
get a report as to the status of the IAs filed for impleading.
Today, a report is placed before us, enclosing the submission of
Xth  Additional  District  Judge,  Ranga  Reddy  District  at
Rajendranagar.
8. IA No.758 of 2023 filed under Order I Rule 10 read with
Section 151 of CPC was filed on 15.09.2023 seeking impleadment of
the petitioners as defendant Nos.5 and 6. The said IA is pending
before the Trial Court.
9. In view of the settlement arrived at by the parties in the
suit, specifically the plaintiff and the defendant Nos.2 and 3, we
are of the opinion that the same shall be recorded, in resolution
of the disputes raised in the suit. We make it clear that the terms
of the settlement bind only the parties to the said settlement.
10. Insofar as the contention of the intervenors are concerned,
those are left open to be agitated in an appropriate forum by way
of appropriate proceedings initiated by those interested, subject
to laws of limitation. The State also interjects and points out
that it has contentions to raise with respect to the property and
the Tahsildar was a party to the suit. The State also would have to
take recourse to proper remedies, permissible in law, if it has to
agitate any interest over the suit scheduled land, again subject to
laws of limitation.
11. Insofar  as  the  parties  to  the  settlement  who  are  the
contesting parties in the suit, the settlement arrived at on
04.05.2026 and made part of this order, shall be recorded and the
suit shall be disposed of in terms of the settlement, drawing up a
4

## Page 197

decree in accordance with that.
12. The Special Leave Petitions stand disposed of with the above
observations and directions.
13. We place on record our gratitude to Hon’ble Mr. Justice L.
Nageswara Rao, Former Judge of this Court, for resolving the
dispute amicably.
14. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

STATE OF HARYANA     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned counsel for the respondent-State of Haryana.
2. Leave granted.
3. In this appeal, appellant has assailed the order
dated 12.03.2026 passed by the High Court of Punjab and
Haryana  at  Chandigarh  (briefly  the  ‘High  Court’
hereinafter), rejecting the regular bail application of
the appellant.
4. Appellant  is  an  accused  in  FIR  No.993/2022
registered at Police Station- Karnal Sadar, District-
Karnal, Haryana under Sections 307, 326 and 34 of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’) and Section
25 of the Arms Act, 1959; Sections 302 and 120B of IPC
were added later on.
5. Prosecution case is that while informant and his
1

## Page 229

uncle Sukhbir were proceeding to their village in a car
driven  by  uncle  Sukhbir,  they  were  intercepted  by
accused Bhupender @ Bhuppi and some other persons. It
is alleged that Bhupender fired a shot from his firearm
upon Sukhbir and his accomplices also joined in the
firing. When people reached the place of occurrence
after hearing gunshots, the assailants fled away. The
injured uncle Sukhbir was taken to hospital. At that
stage, the FIR was lodged. He succumbed to his injuries
and passed away on 24.10.2022, whereafter Sections 302
and 120B of IPC were added.
6. Insofar the appellant is concerned, the allegation
against him is that he was present at the spot along
with the prime accused Bhupender and that one country
made pistol of .315 bore with two live rounds of
ammunition were recovered from him by the police.
7. This Court vide order dated 18.06.2026 had issued
notice pursuant to which respondent-State of Haryana
has filed counter affidavit.
8. Learned counsel for the appellant has drawn the
attention of the Court to the synopsis and submits that
appellant was arrested on 26.10.2022. The charge sheet
was filed on 10.01.2023. Though trial has commenced,
prosecution has cited 41 prosecution witnesses, out of
which only 14 witnesses have been examined thus far.
2

## Page 230

Regarding the allegation against the appellant, he has
referred to page 35B of the Paperbook, which is the
ballistic report and submits that the bullet which hit
the deceased and caused his death was not fired from
the country made pistol, which was recovered following
disclosure statement made by the appellant. Therefore,
there is grave doubt regarding the prosecution case
against the appellant.
9. On the other hand, learned Addl. Advocate General
for the State of Haryana submits that the ballistic
report  is  not  conclusive.  It  is  only  an  opinion.
Further  evidence  will  throw  more  light  on  the
culpability or otherwise of the appellant. Considering
the gruesome nature of the murder, appellant may not be
enlarged on bail, at this stage.
10. Submissions made by learned counsel for the parties
have received the due consideration of the Court.
11. Though we have gone through the materials on record
including the ballistic report, we would not like to
make any comment thereon since the trial is ongoing.
However, we take note of the fact that there is no
specific act allegedly attributed to the appellant. In
any way view of the matter, he has been in custody for
almost 04 years now. Though 14 prosecution witnesses
have been examined out of 41, conclusion of the trial
3

## Page 231

does not appear to be a feasible proposition at this
stage. Therefore, we are inclined to grant bail to the
appellant.
12. Having regard to the above,  t he impugned order
dated 12.03.2026 passed by the High Court is set aside.
Consequently, we direct that the appellant shall be
produced before the concerned Sessions Judge within a
maximum period of 07 days from today, whereafter he
shall be released on bail on such terms and conditions
as may be deemed appropriate.
13. Subject  to  the  above,  the  Criminal  Appeal  is
allowed.
14. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

       IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

VERSUS
SANJEEV KUMAR SINGH       RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Special Appeal No.910 of 2025 presented by the respondent
before the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad was considered by a
Division Bench on 22 nd December, 2006. The operative part of the
order reads as follows:
“Therefore we do not find any material on record to hold that
selection  is  vitiated  due  to  any  alleged  bungling  or  other
irregularity. In view of the aforesaid discussion, Special Appeal
No.592  of  2006  preferred  by  the  respondent-appellants  is
dismissed. The remaining special appeals partly succeed, and
we  direct  the  respondent-authorities  to  fill  in  the  unfilled
vacancies reserved for women candidates and sportsmen ( कु शल
खिलाडी) from suitable candidates of respective category on the
basis of merit list and send them for training and provide all
other benefits, if any as per rules. However we may add here,
since  the  respondents  did  not  hold  recruitment  for  sports
persons in the present selection and we are informed that a
separate  selection  was  held,  therefore,  we  provide  that  the
vacancies remain unfilled from the separate selection held for
sportsmen against 29 vacancies separated from the impugned
selection,  only  those  remaining  vacancies  shall  be  made
1

## Page 239

available  to  the  respective  candidates  of  this  selection.  The
State  Government  is  also  directed  to  comply  with  the  other
directions  given  above  regarding  investigation  into
representation of respective classes in public services within six
months  and  submit  a  compliance  report  to  this  Court
immediately  thereafter  and  not  beyond  31st  July,  2007.  The
Registrar General is directed to send a copy of the judgment to
the Chief Secretary, U.P. Government, Lucknow and Secretary
(Karmik),  U.P.  Government,  Lucknow,  for  information  and
compliance.  The  aforesaid  authorities  are  also  directed  to
communicate  the  principles  laid  down  in  the  judgment  to
various  recruiting  agencies  and  bodies  responsible  for
recruitment in public services to make selection in the light of
the principles laid down in this judgment. The judgments under
appeal are modified to the extent above. There is no order as to
costs.” 
2. We presume, through inadvertence, the Division Bench did not
record that the appeal stands finally disposed of.
3. More  than six years  later, the High  Court noticed  that the
directions  contained  in  the  aforesaid  extract  were  perhaps  not
faithfully implemented by the State of Uttar Pradesh.
4. Proceedings were initiated suo motu and a further order dated
21st December, 2012 was passed reading as follows:
“In  these  circumstances,  and  considering  the  fact  that  the
direction as above relates to a very serious and important issue
regarding  continuance  of  reservation  in  public  services,  in
effective compliance of the Constitution, we do not find any
justification to defer and delay this matter any further. Let this
matter  be  listed  on  11.01.2013  on  which  date  the  Chief
Secretary himself shall file his personal affidavit giving all the
2

## Page 240

details along with the investigation report in compliance of the
above  noted  directions  contained  in  the  judgement  dated
22.12.2006 failing which he shall appear personally before this
Court to explain as to why the direction have not been complied
with, so far, and the persons responsible for the same, and, also
the action, if any, taken against them.”
5. This order of 21st December, 2012, which is the subject matter
of the present appeals, was stayed by this Court by an order dated
09th April, 2013.
6. Having  regard  to  the  nature  of  grievance  voiced  by  the
respondent before the High Court, we are inclined to believe that no
further grievance at his end survives to be addressed. 
7. In such view of the matter, we have taken up the appeals in
his absence.
8. Having regard to the fact that the order dated 21 st December,
2012 merely required the State of Uttar Pradesh to implement the
directions contained in the order dated 22 nd December, 2006, we are
of the considered opinion that interest of justice would be sufficiently
served if the appeals are disposed of with a request to the roster
Bench of the High Court to consider whether, at all, there is any
necessity  to  proceed  with  the  matter  of  implementation  of  the
directions contained in the said order of 22 nd December, 2006. If the
directions given by the High Court have been implemented by the
appellants, the roster Bench may pass an appropriate order and close
the proceedings.
3

## Page 241

9. However,  we  make  it clear that  the  presence  of  the  Chief
Secretary would not be necessary while the High Court proceeds to
consider  the  matter  in  terms  of  this  order.  If  at  all  required,  a
competent officer of the relevant department not below the rank of
Joint Secretary may be asked to file an affidavit to bring on record the
steps  taken  by  the  State  in  pursuance  of  the  order  dated  22nd
December, 2006 as well as the impugned order dated 21 st December,
2012.
10. On  the  aforesaid  terms,  the  appeals  stand  disposed  of.
Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand closed.

CORAM :  HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE VIKRAM NATH
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE SANDEEP MEHTA
For Petitioner(s) : Mr. Prashant Daga, AOR
                   Mr. Purvish Malkhan, Sr. Adv.                   
                   
For Respondent(s) :Mr. Davinder Pal Singh, A.S.G.

      UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                        O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. The petitioner was granted bail by the trial
Court  vide order dated 8 th October, 2004. Condition
Nos. 4 and 5 of the said order read as under:
“(4) The applicant shall not leave India
without prior permission   of the Court;
(5)The  applicant  shall  surrender  his
passport to the Investigating Agency, CBI if
he has any, within 3 days and if he does not
have  the  passport,  he  shall  submit  his
affidavit with regard to the same immediately
1

## Page 259

to the Investigating Agency, CBI giving full
details  of  his  residential  address  and
binding himself immediately report any change
therein.”
3. During the intervening period of about 22
years,  while  facing  the  rigours  of  trial,  the
petitioner moved applications seeking permission to
travel abroad. These applications were allowed, and
the petitioner travelled abroad and returned within
the permitted period.
4. The petitioner’s passport expired on 1 st May,
2026. He, accordingly, approached the High Court by
filing Criminal Misc. Application No. 11212 of 2026,
seeking modification of Condition Nos. 4 and 5 of the
bail order dated 8th October, 2004 passed by the trial
Court,  release  of  his  passport,  permission  for
renewal/re-issuance of passport and permission to
travel abroad for a period of six months.
5. Indisputably, the petitioner has deposited a
sum  of  Rs.  5  lakhs  before  the  trial  Court  as
security.
6. During the course of hearing before the High
Court, the petitioner specifically sought permission
for renewal of his passport for a period of 10 years.
The High Court,  vide  order dated 11 th June, 2026,
allowed the application in part and permitted the
petitioner to travel to the African Continent during
2

## Page 260

the period from 15th June, 2026 to 30th June, 2026. The
learned trial Court was directed to release the
petitioner’s passport for the said purpose, subject
to the petitioner depositing a sum of Rs.50,000/-
with the trial Court along with one surety of the
like amount.
7. The High Court, however, did not advert to the
petitioner's prayer for renewal of the passport for
10 years. Aggrieved, he has approached this Court by
way of the instant special leave petition.
8. Shri Davinder Pal Singh, learned Additional
Solicitor  General,  appeared  on  behalf  of  the
respondents and waived service.
9. Shri Singh submitted that the CBI does not
have any objection to the prayer for renewal/re-
issuance of the passport.  However, he urges that the
passport issuing authority may be directed to deposit
the renewed passport directly with the trial Court
and, in the event the petitioner desires to travel
abroad, he may be required to move an appropriate
application before the trial Court seeking release of
the passport and permission to travel.
10. We have heard and considered the submissions
advanced at bar and perused the material available on
record.
3

## Page 261

11. Having regard to the fact that the petitioner
has been facing trial for the last about 22 years
and, during this entire period, has not been shown to
have violated any of the conditions imposed while
granting him bail, we are of the considered view that
there  is  no  reason  whatsoever  as  to  why  the
petitioner’s prayer for renewal of passport for 10
years should not be acceded to.
12. Accordingly,  we  direct  that  the  passport
authority concerned shall deal with the petitioner's
application for renewal/re-issuance of passport for a
period of 10 years, in accordance with the prevailing
procedure and rules.
13. Upon receipt of the renewed/fresh passport,
the petitioner shall deposit the same with the trial
Court.  The  petitioner  shall  also  furnish  an
undertaking before the trial Court that he shall not
leave  the  country  without  obtaining  its  prior
permission.
14. The special leave petition is disposed of
accordingly.
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.
(SONIA BHASIN) (RANJANA SHAILEY)

1 appellant-institution

at Jodhpur 3 relying upon the judgment and order of even date (17 th

by it. Both the judgment(s) dated 17 th August, 2016 are under challenge
in these appeals by special leave, granted on 15th October, 2024.   
3. Facts giving rise to the special appeals have been delineated by
the High Court in the impugned judgment while disposing of D. B. Civil
Special Appeal (Writ) No.415 of 2014; in view thereof, we do not repeat
the facts herein. Suffice it to note that the appellant-institution on and
from 2010-11 came to be governed by the statutes of the Rajasthan
Ayurved  University,  Jodhpur  which  fixed  the  retirement  age  of  the
employees  at  60  (sixty)  years.  Submission  made  on  behalf  of  the
appellant-institution before the High Court, also supported by the State
of  Rajasthan,  was  that  the  appellant-institution  is  governed  by  the
Rajasthan Ayurvedic Donation Assistance Rules, 1972 5. Incidentally, in
terms of the 1972 Rules, the retirement age of the employees is 58
years. However, such submission was not accepted by the High Court.
4.  We  are,  however,  of  the  view  that  the  High  Court  (for  the
reasons it assigned) was right in not accepting the submission of the
appellant-institution that it was governed by the 1972 Rules. Appellant-
institution  had  on  an earlier  occasion  opted out  of  the  1972  Rules,
whereupon it came to be regulated by the statutes of the Rajasthan
Ayurved University, Jodhpur.

the Single Judge’s judgment, the appellant-institution must be deemed
to have accepted the same and the appeals filed by the appellant-
institution before us, from the decision on the State’s intra-court appeal,
is not maintainable. 
6. For the twin reasons referred to above, we find no reason to
entertain the civil appeals.
7. The civil appeals are, accordingly, dismissed.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
9. No costs.
10. The  order  of  the  Single  Judge  may  be  implemented  by  the
appellant-institution, if not already implemented, within 4 weeks.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioner is an advocate practising before the Supreme
Court. He has filed the instant petition, purportedly in public
interest, seeking the following directions:
“a.  Issue a writ in the nature of mandamus, order,
direction  or  any  other  appropriate  writ  directing
Respondent Nos. 1 to 3 to consider, within a time-bound
period, preferably within three months, the Petitioner's
representation  dated  22.06.2026  for  framing  a
constitutionally  compliant  mechanism  for  urgent
reporting, preservation, judicial/legal review and URL-
specific  disabling  of  access  within  India  in  cases
involving:
i. specific threats of physical violence, sexual violence
or death;
ii. doxxing creating reasonable apprehension of harm;
1

## Page 269

iii.   unauthorised  disclosure  of  private  details,
photographs, school details, location data or identity
markers of minor children;
iv.  non-consensual intimate, morphed, synthetic or Al-
generated content;
v.  non-consensual  deepfake  or  digitally  manipulated
impersonation causing immediate grave harm to safety,
dignity, livelihood or reputation;
b. Pending such consideration, issue limited interim
directions that any aggrieved person may approach the
jurisdictional  District  Court,  High  Court  or  such
designated duty court as may be notified by the concerned
High Court for urgent URL-specific relief in the above
categories;
c. Direct that such applications, where supported by
affidavit/verified  identity  and  precise
URLs/screenshots/timestamps  wherever  possible,  may  be
considered expeditiously, preferably within 24 to 48
hours, after recording reasons;
d. Direct that any interim order disabling access shall
be:
i. URL-specific;
ii.reasoned; 
iii. confined to the content complained of;
iv. limited to disabling access within India unless
exceptional  reasons  are  separately  recorded  by  a
competent court;
v. subject to preservation of evidence;
vi. subject to notice to the uploader where identifiable;
vii. subject to post-order hearing within a reasonable
short period;
e. Direct intermediaries, upon receipt of a court order
or lawful order of competent authority, to preserve the
2

## Page 270

complained-of  content,  URLs,  timestamps,  associated
records and relevant metadata for a period consistent
with law, without public access to harmful content and
subject to privacy and due process safeguards;
f.  Direct  that  preserved  information  shall  not  be
disclosed to private complainants except under lawful
order of a competent court or competent authority;
g. Clarify that nothing in the directions shall authorise
prior  restraint  or  emergency  takedown  of  political
speech, journalism, public-interest reporting, satire,
parody, fair criticism, opinion, academic commentary,
legal  commentary,  criticism  of  public  officials,
criticism  of  public  institutions  or  criticism  of
government policy;
h. Clarify that ordinary defamation disputes involving
contested facts, fair comment, public interest, satire,
opinion or journalistic material shall ordinarily be left
to regular civil or criminal remedies and shall not be
treated as emergency takedown cases merely because the
speech is harsh, inconvenient, unpopular or offensive;
i. Direct that any complainant who knowingly files a
false,  malicious  or  suppressive  complaint  may  be
subjected  to  costs,  perjury  proceedings  or  other
appropriate legal consequences;
j. Direct that if the content is found to be protected
speech or the complaint is found to be mala fide, the
order disabling access shall be vacated and restoration
shall be directed, subject to law;
k. Direct Respondent Nos. 1 to 3 to consider constituting
an  expert  consultative  committee  comprising
representatives from MeitY, MHA, Ministry of Law and
Justice, NCW, NCPCR, CERT-In, cyber law experts, free
speech experts, privacy experts, child rights experts,
women's safety experts, intermediary representatives and
civil society organisations;
l. Direct Respondent Nos. 1 to 3 to place before this
Hon'ble Court an affidavit indicating:
3

## Page 271

i. the existing framework for emergency response to
online threats, doxxing, child exposure and deepfake
impersonation;
ii. whether any proposal for amendment of rules or
creation of an urgent mechanism is under consideration;
iii.  the  existing  average  timeline  for  grievance
resolution in the above categories;
iv. the safeguards available to protect political speech,
journalism, satire, criticism and opinion;
v. steps taken for preservation of digital evidence;
m. Pass any other or further order which this Hon'ble
Court may deem fit and proper in the interest of justice,
constitutional governance and protection of fundamental
rights.”
2. In sum and substance, the petitioner seeks creation of a URL-
specific, judicially supervised emergency mechanism against grave
unlawful digital harms, which include threats of violence, doxxing,
unauthorised  disclosure  of  children’s  details,  non-consensual
intimate/deepfake content and harmful digital impersonation etc.
It is submitted that such cybercrimes grossly violate fundamental
rights to equality, speech, privacy, dignity and life and are
seriously impacting the same, without any timely, effective state
protection.  A  comparison  has  been  drawn  with  international
frameworks to urge that various initiatives are required to be
taken urgently by the authority in order to control the menace of
such unlawful digital activities.
3. We  find  that  the  petitioner  has  raised  these  issues
comprehensively in a representation dated 22.06.2026 addressed to
the concerned Ministries of the Union of India. Since the remedial
4

## Page 272

actions are required to be taken by the addressee authorities, we
dispose of this petition at this stage with a direction to
respondent Nos. 1 to 3 and all other stakeholders to look into the
issues raised by the petitioner in his representation and take such
remedial measures as may be required in accordance with law.
4. The  Writ  Petition  stands  disposed  of,  with  pending
application(s), if any.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.       OF 2026
(arising out of SLP(C) NO.10602/2026)
K. RAMABHADRAN APPELLANT(S)
                              VERSUS
M/S. LUXURY SANDS KERALA PRIVATE LIMITED &
ORS.
RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The instant appeal arises out of the Impugned Order dated
30.06.2025 passed by the High Court of Kerala at Ernakulam
(“High Court”) in Arbitration Request No. 150/2024, whereby the
Appellant’s application under Section 11(6) of the Arbitration
and Conciliation Act, 1996 (“the Act”) for appointment of a Sole
Arbitrator was dismissed on the ground that the claim was ex
facie and hopelessly time-barred.
3. To reiterate the facts briefly, the Appellant entered into a
Memorandum  of  Understanding  (“MoU”)  dated  24.06.2009  with
Respondent No. 1, represented by Respondent No. 2 as its
Managing Director, for purchase of a metal crusher unit together
with approximately 35 acres of quarry land at Elanji, Ernakulam
District, for a total consideration of Rs. 17.15 crores. For
this, the Appellant paid an advance of Rs. 10 lakhs. The initial
time of performance was upto 10.08.2009 which was extended till
30.11.2009 by a further MoU dated 06.11.2009, pursuant to which
the Appellant paid an additional advance sale consideration of
Rs. 1 crore. Clause 20 of the MoU dated 24.06.2009 stipulates
1

## Page 284

that “any dispute arising out of the MoU is to be settled by
arbitration”.
4. It is the Appellant’s case that disputes arose when it was
discovered that the Respondents possessed only about 20 acres of
the subject land, instead of the agreed-upon 35 acres, which led
to the Appellant’s inability to purchase the property within the
extended time. Accordingly, the Appellant filed Arbitration O.P.
No. 266/2010 under Section 9 of the Act before the District
Judge, Ernakulam, seeking an injunction against the Respondents
from alienating the subject property. This petition came to be
dismissed on 17.04.2010 as there was no valid arbitration
clause.
5. The  Appellant  challenged  this  order  through  Arbitration
Appeal No. 26/2010 before the High Court, aggrieved by the
finding regarding the non-existence of a valid arbitration
clause.  Vide the judgment dated 22.06.2023, the High Court
clarified that the District Court’s finding concerning the
validity of the arbitration clause was only a  prima facie
opinion  and  shall  not  bind  the  parties  in  subsequent
proceedings.
6. Pursuant to this clarification, the Appellant issued a Notice
Invoking  Arbitration  dated  02.04.2024  to  the  Respondents,
proposing the name of a Sole Arbitrator and seeking a refund of
the advance amount of Rs. 1.10 crores with interest at the rate
of 18% p.a., as well as damages/costs.
7. The Respondents, however, through a reply dated 16.04.2024
denied any breach of the MoU, asserted that the claim was time-
2

## Page 285

barred, and claimed that there was no valid arbitration clause.
This prompted the Appellant to file Arbitration Request No.
150/2024 under Section 11(6) of the Act before the High Court,
which came to be dismissed  vide the impugned judgment dated
30.06.2025, relying on this Court’s decision in  Aslam Ismail
Khan Deshmukh v. ASAP Fluids Pvt. Ltd., (2025) 1 SCC 502.
8. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the
material placed on record.
9. The existence of Clause 20 of the MoU dated 24.06.2009,
providing for reference of disputes to arbitration is not in
dispute. Indeed, the High Court, while disposing of Arbitration
Appeal No. 26/2010  vide the judgment dated 22.06.2023, has
itself held that the District Court’s doubts regarding the
validity  of  the  arbitration  clause  were  only  prima  facie
observations in proceedings under Section 9 of the Act and were
not binding on subsequent proceedings. Therefore, having regard
to the limited scope of enquiry contemplated under Section 11(6)
of the Act, we are of the view that the question of limitation
raised  by  the  Respondents,  being  an  arbitrable  question
dependent upon appreciation of facts, ought to be left for
determination by the Arbitral Tribunal.
10. In view of the facts and circumstances recorded above,
the instant appeal is allowed and the Impugned Order is set
aside. We, accordingly, appoint Hon’ble Mr. Justice A. M.
Shaffique, former Judge of the High Court of Kerala as the Sole
Arbitrator  to  adjudicate  the  disputes  between  the  parties
arising  out  of  the  MoUs  dated  24.06.2009  and  06.11.2009,
3

## Page 286

including the question of limitation raised by the Respondents,
which is left open for determination by the learned Arbitrator.
The seat and venue of arbitration shall be Ernakulam, Kerala.
11. The Arbitrator shall have the liberty to fix his own
fees.

1. The  present  Special  Leave  Petition  calls  in
question  the  correctness  of  the  judgment  dated  19 th
September, 2025 passed by the High Court at Calcutta in
1

## Page 289

CRR No.2028 of 2025.  By the said judgment, the High
Court has dismissed the revision of the petitioners.  The
revision itself was against the order of the Appellate
Court confirming the conviction and sentence passed by
the Metropolitan Magistrate, 14 th Court at Calcutta.  The
Metropolitan  Magistrate  had,  in  a  Section  138
proceedings, initiated by respondent No.2 against the
petitioners after convicting the petitioners, sentenced
the petitioners to pay a fine amount of Rs.17,50,000/-
(Rupees seventeen lakhs fifty thousand) and in default
ordered  petitioner  Nos.  2  and  3  to  undergo  simple
imprisonment for two years and further ordered attachment
against petitioner No.1.  
2. It is undisputed before us that out of the sum of
Rs.17,50,000/- (Rupees seventeen lakhs fifty thousand), a
sum of Rs.6,50,000/- (Rupees six lakhs fifty thousand)
has already been paid to the complainant.
3. Ms. Karuna Nundy, learned senior counsel appearing
for the second respondent/complainant does not dispute
this  fact.  That  leaves  a  balance  of  Rs.11,00,000/-
(Rupees eleven lakhs).
4. Ms. Reshmi Ghosh, learned counsel appearing for the
petitioners, on instructions, submits that given some
time, the petitioners would deposit the balance amount of
Rs.11,00,000/- (Rupees eleven lakhs).  Learned counsel
prays for three months’ time to deposit the aforesaid
amount.
2

## Page 290

5. Having  considered  the  submission,  we  pass  the
following order:
(a) The  petitioners  shall  on  or  before  15 th
September,  2026  deposit  in  this  Court  a  sum  of
Rs.5,50,000/- (Rupees five lakhs fifty thousand);
(b) Further, the petitioners shall on or before
27th October,  2026  deposit  the  balance  amount  of
Rs.5,50,000/- (Rupees five lakhs fifty thousand);
(c) On  each  of  such  deposit  being  made,  the
Registry shall keep the amounts in a short-term fixed
deposit with any nationalized bank on auto-renewal basis;
(d) The petitioner Nos. 2 and 3 shall on their
behalf  and  on  behalf  of  petitioner  No.1  file  an
undertaking before this Court stating therein that they
will strictly comply with the above schedule of payment.
Such undertaking shall be filed on or before 24 th August,
2026; and
(e) It  is  made  clear  that  the  breach  of  the
undertaking will result in serious consequences.
6. List for recording compliance with regard to the
first installment on 18th September, 2026.

27th January, 2026 shall continue to operate till the next

2. We have considered the matters in depth.
3. The present petitions have been filed against the interim
order dated 21.08.2025 passed by the High Court of Uttarakhand in
WPSS No.1177 of 2025 and WPSS No.1094 of 2025, by which the
termination of respondent no.5 vide order dated 09.07.2025 passed
by the Executive Officer, Nagar Panchayat Swargashram Jonk, Pauri
Garhwal, has been stayed. 
4. The petitioner was the person at whose behest, the matter was
initiated  resulting  in  such  termination  of  the  service  of
respondent no.5. This Court by order dated 19.09.2025 had stayed
the operation of the interim order dated 21.08.2025 passed by the

High Court of Uttarakhand at Nainital in WPSS No.1094 of 2025 and
WPSS No.1177 of 2025.
5. Today, Mr. Gaurav Bhatia, learned Senior Additional Advocate
General for the respondent no.1-State of Uttarakhand submits that
the State has taken a pro-active and prompt action in the matter
and the initial order of termination dated 09.07.2025 has been
given effect to. It was further submitted that the State has taken
the issue seriously and would not be found lacking in taking strict
action in the matter.
6. Having considered the aforesaid position, we find no reason to
keep the petitions pending. As the main matter on merits is still
pending before the High Court, the present petitions stand disposed
of with liberty to the parties to move before the High Court for
expeditious disposal of the Writ Petitions.
7. We make it clear that we have not expressed any opinion on the
merits of the matters and the High Court while hearing the Writ
Petitions shall consider all issues on facts as well as on law
raised by the parties concerned and take an independent decision,
in accordance with law, without being prejudiced by any observation
being made in any order by this Court in present proceedings. The
order dated 19.09.2025 passed by this Court staying the interim
order dated 21.08.2025 passed by the High Court against grant of
stay of termination, is made absolute till the final disposal of
the WPSS No.1094 of 2025 and WPSS No.1177 of 2025.

Date : 04-08-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE ARAVIND KUMAR
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE VIPUL M. PANCHOLI
For Petitioner(s) : Mr. Gaurav Goel, AOR
                   
For Respondent(s) :Mr. Jayant Bhushan, Sr. Adv.
                   Mr. Joseph Pookkatt, Adv.
                   Mr. Nilesh Sharma, Adv.
                   Mr. Dhawesh Pahuja, Adv.
                   Ms. Awantika Manohar, Adv.
                   M/s AP & J Chambers, AOR
                   
                   
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. This is a classic case and mirror to the fact that the parties instead of playing
at the goalpost are playing in the outer field, and we say so for the brief reasons
indicated hereinbelow. On account of parties not being ad idem on issue arising
out of a contract dated 14.12.2009 / 19.12.2009, said differences blossomed
1

## Page 313

itself into a dispute resulting in the parties igniting the arbitration clause which
culminated into an arbitral award dated 02.02.2018. It is apt and appropriate to
note at this juncture itself that the respondent herein, in order to substantiate
its claim, produced certain documents namely 60 documents, the production of
which was opposed by the petitioner herein. The arbitral tribunal, by its order
dated  05.12.2015  (Anexure  P-22),  allowed  the  respondent  to  place  those
documents on record on payment of costs and directed that documents are to
be proved as per law. In the midst of recording of oral evidence, an order came
to be passed on 25.01.2016, (Annexure P-23) as under:
“The  Tribunal  had  started  recording  the  statement  of  the
Claimant's witness. However, after some cross examination, it was
agreed between the parties that there is no need of recording any
oral  evidence  and  the  matter  can  straight  away  be  fixed  for
arguments.  It  is  also  agreed  that  whatever  oral  evidence  was
recorded today will not be read.
While fixing dates, it was noticed that the venue at the Delhi
International  Arbitration  Centre  is  not  available  till  middle  of
March-2016. Parties, therefore, agreed that matter may be fixed
for arguments in the office of Arbitral Tribunal.
In view of the above, the matter will come up for arguments
on 25.02.2016 at 3PM, 29.02.2016 at 5PM and on 03.03.2016 at
3PM for arguments in the office of the Arbitral Tribunal at A-27,
Defence Colony, New Delhi. The E-mails placed on record by the
parties will be read without any formal proof. It will be appreciated
if the parties file a brief synopsis of their respective case at least
three days before the date fixed for arguments.”
Subsequently, final arguments could not be concluded on account of the
sad demise of the learned sole arbitrator, resulting in substitution of a new
arbitrator  and  after  reconstitution  of  the  arbitral  tribunal,  as  noticed
hereinabove, passed an award came to be passed on 02.02.2018 whereunder a
sum of Rs.2,29,36,249/- with interest at 18% per annum, and costs of Rs. 10
lakhs, came to be awarded in favor of the petitioner herein. 
2. Being aggrieved by the same, the respondent herein has filed a petition
under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, for setting aside
the same on various grounds urged therein. When the matter was at the stage
of arguments, the petitioner herein filed an application under Section 34(4) of
2

## Page 314

the Act, inter alia seeking for adjourning the proceedings for a fixed period of
time, in order to give the arbitral tribunal an opportunity to resume the arbitral
proceedings to eliminate the grounds of challenge regarding purported non-
consideration of the respondent's documents (60 documents), if any, for setting
aside the arbitral award, as has been urged in the petition filed under Section
34 of the Act. By the impugned order, the learned Judge has held that Section
34(4) cannot be invoked to enable an arbitral tribunal to reopen the conclusion
reached. Hence, this petition.
3. The learned counsel senior counsels appearing for the parties have stood to
their grounds as urged in their respective pleadings and it was vehemently
contended by the learned senior counsel appearing for petitioner that in the
light  of  the  purported  60  documents,  having  not  been  considered  by  the
tribunal, had vitiated the award as canvassed by the respondent herein, is an
issue which will have to be thrashed out by examining the said documents itself
by the tribunal and this would give less scope for interference under Section 34
of the Act. Per contra, Shri Jayant Bhushan, learned senior counsel appearing for
the respondent, would support the impugned order and prays for dismissal of
the petition.
4. Having heard the learned senior counsels appearing for the parties and on
perusal of the entire case papers, it would not detain us for too long to brush
aside the contentions raised by the learned senior counsel appearing for the
petitioner, for two reasons, firstly, the order dated 05.12.2015 passed by the
arbitral tribunal at first instance, would clearly go to show that the respondent
herein was permitted to place the documents on record on payment of costs
and undisputedly the cost has been paid and received. In such circumstances, it
is not open to the petitioner to reagitate the said issue, or in other words, to
contend that the application ought not to have been allowed. Secondly, the
tribunal by its record of proceedings dated 25.01.2016 has clearly recorded that
oral evidence was unnecessary and fixed the matter for final arguments. This
would only indicate that obviously the tribunal intended to examine the said
documents.
3

## Page 315

5. At this juncture, a pointed question was posed to the learned senior counsel
appearing for the petitioner as to whether the petitioner had disputed the very
existence of the documents or the contents of the documents? And the learned
senior counsel fairly submitted, on instructions, that it is only the contents of
the documents which have been disputed. If it were to be so, it was the duty of
the tribunal to have examined the veracity of the said documents. However, we
do not propose to enter into any discussion with regard to the same for the
simple  reason  that  these  are  the  contentions  which  have  been  urged  and
countered by the parties in pending Section 34 proceedings and said issue is
still at large. Any scrutiny or examination of the said issue by this Court will
definitely prejudice the rights of either of the parties. Hence, we leave at it.
6. In view of the purported 60 documents having not been considered by the
tribunal, according to the respondent herein, has vitiated the award. In what
manner it has so prejudiced the rights of the parties, is an issue which will have
to be thrashed out by examining the documents which are on record, by the
Court which is adjudicating the petition under section 34. As such, we do not
see any infirmity in the impugned order and judgment which would warrant our
interference at the hands of this Court. Hence, the Special Leave Petition is
dismissed. Parties to bear their costs.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
(RASHI GUPTA)                                   (AVGV RAMU)
COURT MASTER (SH)                             COURT MASTER (NSH)

refers to the recent status report filed on behalf of the State and
points out that possession of land measuring 23.17 acres has

5.27 acres will be handed over by 31.08.2026. The delay occurred on
account of the delay in demolition of existing buildings thereon,
some of which were occupied by the staff of the Government as well
as High Court.
2. The relevant portions of the sanction of plans and tender, as
reproduced in the status report filed on behalf of State of
Maharashtra, are extracted hereunder:
“b. Sanction of Plans:
The conceptual plans for the New High Court building have
been approved by the Steering Committee on 23 rd July 2026
taking  into  consideration  requirements  of  the  Court
Halls, Administrative Offices, Bar Association and all
other  facilities.  The  Architect  submitted  following
timelines before the Steering Committee.
The Architect and Public Works Department have suggested
following timelines:
Sr. 
No.
Particulars Timeline
1. Mechanical,  Electrical  and  Plumbing
(MEP)  drawings,  structural  layout
(columns, beams position)
2 weeks
2. RCC designs (columns, beams, grade of
concrete etc.)
3 weeks
3. Estimates
Quantities, Rates, (DSR and non DSR
rates),  Internal  finishing  and
electricals
2 weeks
4. Tender amendment (4 volumes)
Volume 1 : Request for proposal
Volume 2 : General contract Conditions
Volume 3 : Technical specifications &
design basis reports
1 week

## Page 334

Volume 4 : Drawings and schedule of
finishes
Thus, the total time required for floating the details on
Tender portal is 8 weeks.
The Steering Committee has acceded to the said request.
c. Tender:
After the plans are finalized by the Architect and placed
before the Steering Committee, tender will be updated and
the process of receiving Bids will begin as follows:
i) Tender, after the above process, will be opened for
submission of bids. The time for pre-bid meetings
and submissions will be approximately 25 to 45 days.
ii) After which the following stages of tender will
occur:
a. Technical scrutiny
b. Shortlisting of bidders
c. Opening of financial bids
iii) The tender documents will be placed before the
Steering Committee.
iv) List of shortlisted bidders will be placed before
the Steering Committee.
v) There will be no Joint Venture bidder and the
Selected Bidder will be allowed to appoint Sub-
Contractor only for internal works and furnishing
under the overall responsibility of the Selected
Bidder. Areas which will be permitted to be sub-
contracted will be clearly identified.”
3. It is informed by Mr. Sathe, learned Advocate General, that
some of the requisite permissions have already been applied for and
that, in any event, the tender process will be completed within
eight weeks after floating details of the tender portal are
finalised.
4. It is stated that the finalisation of tender and selection of
contractor shall be completed before 31.12.2026.

## Page 356

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.   3770   OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO. 12127/2026)
VIJAY DHRUW      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF CHHATTISGARH     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of
Chhattisgarh.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant  takes  exception  to  the  order  dated
30.06.2026 passed by the High Court of Chhattisgarh at
Bilaspur  (briefly  the  ‘High  Court’  hereinafter),
rejecting  the  regular  bail  application  of  the
appellant.
4. Appellant  is  an  accused  in  FIR  No.150/2025
registered  at  Police  Station-  Mainpur,  District-
Gariyaband,  Chhattisgarh  under  Sections  137(2)  and
64(2)(m) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (for
short,  ‘BNS’)  read  with  Sections  4  and  6  of  the
Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012.
1

## Page 357

5. Prosecution case is that father of the prosecutrix
lodged First Information Report before the concerned
police station alleging that his minor daughter was
kidnapped by some unknown person. Victim was recovered
from the house of the appellant. It is alleged that
appellant had indulged in physical relationship with
the victim.
6. This Court vide order dated 13.07.2026 had issued
notice.
7. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that both
the appellant and the victim are of impressionable age
and had developed a relationship, pursuant to which
they had eloped. On a query by the Court, he submits
that the age of the appellant would be 19 years.
Appellant is in custody since 06.11.2025. Therefore,
appellant may be granted bail.
8. On the contrary, learned Addl. Advocate General for
the State of Chhattisgarh submits that the victim is 16
years of age. That apart, trial is proceeding at a
reasonable pace. Out of 20 cited witnesses, 07 have
already  been  examined.  05  material  witnesses  still
remain  to  be  examined.  Therefore,  at  this  stage,
appellant may not be enlarged on bail.
9. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and
on due consideration, we are inclined to grant bail to
2

## Page 358

the appellant. While the trial is going on, the same
does not appear to be in any way near conclusion, at
this stage. In the meanwhile, appellant is in jail
since 06.11.2025. Both appellant and the victim girl
are known to each other.
10. Having regard to the above,  t he impugned order
dated 30.06.2026 passed by the High Court is set aside.
Consequently, we direct that the appellant shall be
produced before the concerned Trial Court within a
maximum period of 07 days from today, whereafter he
shall be released on bail on such terms and conditions
as may be deemed appropriate.
11. Subject  to  the  above,  the  Criminal  Appeal  is
allowed.
12. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.
…………………………………………………...J.
      
   [UJJAL BHUYAN]
…………………………………………………...J.
     [ATUL S. CHANDURKAR]
NEW DELHI;
11th AUGUST, 2026.

CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.   3771   OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO. 12776/2026)
GYA PRASAD TIWARI      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of  Madhya
Pradesh.
2. Leave granted.
3. Though a letter has been circulated on behalf of
the  respondent-State  of  Madhya  Pradesh  seeking
adjournment, we are not inclined to grant further time
to the respondent, considering the peculiar facts and
circumstances of the case.
4. Appellant has been convicted by the Trial Court
under Sections 419, 420, 467 and 471/120 of the Indian
Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’) and sentenced to
undergo Rigorous Imprisonment (for short, ‘R.I.’) for
05 years.
5. Appellant has assailed his conviction and sentence
1

## Page 361

before the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur
(briefly  the  ‘High  Court’  hereinafter)  in  Criminal
Appeal  No.8718/2025.  Along  with  the  appeal,  an
application was filed by the appellant for suspension
of sentence and grant of bail. However, by the impugned
order dated 30.06.2026, the prayer of the appellant has
been rejected.
6. Notice in this case was issued on 27.07.2026.
7. We are inclined to suspend the sentence and grant
bail to the appellant for the following reasons:
(i) Appellant has been sentenced to undergo R.I. for 05
years. He has already undergone about one year of
incarceration.
(ii) Appeal  is  of  the  year  2025.  Considering  the
pendency of Criminal Appeals in the particular High
Court, it is not likely that the related appeal will be
heard in the near future.
(iii) There is a good arguable case on merit.
(iv)  Appellant is 80 years old.
8. We find that while the High Court had noted the
fact that appellant is 80 years old, yet the High Court
not only dismissed the application seeking suspension
of sentence and grant of bail but also directed the
appeal to be listed in  DUE COURSE . We may also note
that appellant had made one application after the other
2

## Page 362

but failed to find any response from the High Court.
This is unfortunate to say the least.
9. Having regard to the above,  t he impugned order
dated 30.06.2026 passed by the High Court is set aside.
Consequently, while suspending the sentence, we direct
that  the  appellant  shall  be  produced  before  the
concerned Magistrate within a maximum period of 07 days
from today, whereafter he shall be released on bail on
such terms and conditions as may be deemed appropriate.
10. Subject  to  the  above,  the  Criminal  Appeal  is
allowed.
11. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.   3768   OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO. 6506/2026)
GITA DEVI @ GITA KUMARI      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF BIHAR       RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned counsel for the respondent-State of Bihar.
2. Leave granted.
3. This  appeal  takes  exception  to  the  order  dated
24.02.2026 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Patna
(briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting the
prayer for anticipatory bail of the appellant.
4. It is stated that appellant has been arrayed as an
accused in FIR No.285/2022 registered at Police Station-
Paliganj, District- Patna, Bihar under Sections 419, 420,
409 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short,
‘IPC’).
5. Prosecution case, in brief, is that as a Ward member,
appellant had allegedly embezzled government money of
Rs.13,78,000/- meant for execution of government schemes.
6. This Court, by order dated 27.04.2026, had issued
notice and granted interim protection to the appellant
1

## Page 369

subject  to  the  appellant  co-operating  with  the
investigation.
7. Learned  counsel  for  the  appellant  submits  that
appellant is a woman. As a Ward member, she is not
directly involved in the execution of government schemes.
In any case, substantial work has been executed. No case
under the aforesaid provisions of law are, therefore, made
out. She has clean antecedents. That apart, pursuant to
the interim protection granted by this Court, appellant
had approached the concerned investigating officer on a
number of occasions but her examination has not been
carried out.
8. On  the  other  hand,  learned  counsel  for  the
respondent-State  of  Bihar  submits  from  the  counter
affidavit that appellant has not co-operated with the
investigation.  Though  attempts  were  made  by  the
investigating  officer  to  contact  her,  she  remained
completely unreachable.
9. In response, learned counsel for the appellant has
referred to Paragraph No.25 of the rejoinder affidavit and
submits that on 30.06.2026, 21.07.2026, 22.07.2026 and
23.07.2026, she along with her husband, had visited the
police station with a view to join the investigation.
However, no steps have been taken by the investigating
officer in this regard.
10. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and on
due consideration, we are of the view that the interim
2

## Page 370

protection  granted  by  this  Court  vide  order  dated
27.04.2026 should be made absolute.
11. That being the position, we set aside the impugned
order dated 24.02.2026 passed by the High Court and make
the  order  dated  27.04.2026  absolute.  However,  the
appellant  shall  continue  to  co-operate  with  the
investigation of the case.
12. Consequently, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
13. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Learned counsel for the petitioner has placed on record the
relevant information in a tabulated form, depicting the number of
commercial cases pending as on 31.01.2025 and the corresponding
infrastructure that has been provided for the commercial courts. 
2. It seems to us that the information needs to be updated, at
least upto the date of 31.01.2026, along with the details of the
infrastructure  that  has  been  provided  so  far.  We  have  also
impressed upon learned counsel for the petitioner to collect the
data with respect to the state-wise trend of growth in commercial
litigation and to have an estimated requirement of additional
commercial  courts  in  such  States.  The  consideration  of  that
information may enable the issuance of appropriate directions for
establishment of additional commercial courts.
3. For the purpose of establishment of additional commercial
courts as contemplated above, it is necessary to ensure the
presence of the State Governments in these proceedings. Let notice
be, therefore, issued to all the States, who are already impleaded
as party respondents, returnable on 24.09.2026.  
3

## Page 375

4. The States may be served through their Standing Counsel in the
Supreme Court or through their respective Advocates General.  
5. The information collated by the learned counsel for the
petitioner in the tabulated form is taken on record. Let a soft
copy thereof be deposited with the Registry. The Registry is
directed to furnish a copy of the said information in a digital,
tabulated form to all the High Courts, seeking their response,
before the date fixed.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. It has transpired from the averments made in the Writ Petition
that in the light of the recommendations made by the Parliamentary
Standing Committee in its 139th report on health and family welfare,
3

## Page 379

17 States and Union Territories have already notified Cancer as a
“notified disease”.  These recommendations are to the following
effect:
“The  Committee  notes  that  Cancer  is  still  not
classified as a notifiable disease which results in
underreporting of cancer deaths.  The Committee notes
that ambiguity on the actual casuse of death is a
major hurdle in data collection.  It has been brought
to the notice of the Committee that many a times;
death is simply recorded as cardio-respiratory failure
without mentioning the actual cause of death.  The
Committee is of the view that an accurate mortality
database  in  the  hospital  information  system  will
improve cancer registry, follow up and outcome data.
The Committee therefore agrees with the suggestion of
TMC that Cancer must be classified as a notifiable
disease so that the cancer deaths are mandatorily
required to be reported to the Government machinery.  
The Committee strongly believes that making Cancer a
“Notified  Disease”  will  surely  ensure  a  robust
database  of  the  cancer  deaths  but  also  help  in
determining the accurate incidence and prevalence of
Cancer in the country.  It will also help in analyzing
the risk factors, implementing screening programs, and
allocating  proper  resources  to  improve  cancer
outcomes.   Data  collected  can  also  be  used  to
formulate  standard  treatment  guidelines  that  will
further strengthen the continuum of cancer care.  The
Committee further recommends that to streamline and
improve data collection a CoWIN-like web portal for
the  registration,  real-time  data  collection,
counselling,  supportive  resources  for  cancer  care
along with interactive tools can be created by the
Government.  The portal can also be equipped to aid
those affected by cancer by guiding them through the
treatment and management journey.”
2. We,  consequently,  direct  the  remaining  States  and  Union
Territories also to consider the above stated recommendations and
take an appropriate decision.  Compliance affidavits be filed.
3. List on 21.09.2026.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The learned counsel appearing for the respondent-husband virtually,
makes a request to permit the respondent-husband to address the Court. Since,
respondent is already represented by a counsel, permitting him to address the
Court is not warranted. Hence, his request stands rejected.
2. This  Court  by  Order  dated  20.07.2026  had  taken  note  of  the
statement made by the learned counsel appearing for the respondent-husband
that he is not in a position to travel to India. In view of the same his passport
has been cancelled. In the present scenario, the only option left for the Union Of
India is to take steps as indicated in our Order dated 26.08.2025 which is to the
following effect:
“Today, a note has been submitted by learned counsel for the
Union of India, whereunder suggestions for way forward has been
put forth and it reads thus:
II. Suggestions for Way Forward:
A.  For  presence  of  the  Accused/Contemnor  for  next  date  of
hearing;  Court  may  ask  Ministry  of  Home  Affairs  serve  to
summons through U.S.A. Authorities under the bilateral treaty on
Mutual Legal Assistance in criminal matters (MLAT).
B.  If  the  accused  has  an  Indian  passport,  Court  may  direct
revocation of his passport by MEA and pursue deportation with
U.S.A. authorities.
C. Extradition from U.S.A. in this case may not be feasible as
contempt of Court alone is not an extraditable offence (minimum
punishment should be 01 years for extraditon).
D. India is not a party to Hague Convention on Child abduction by
Parents, hence these countries (100 plus including U.S.A.) may not
be made a party to answer to Court on how he left India."
3

## Page 387

3. The Union of India is at liberty to take steps in accordance with the
aforestated  note  submitted  to  this  Court  to  secure  the  presence  of  the
respondent-husband.
4. List on 15.10.2026.

O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. There are two Civil Appeals before us. The first Appeal
arises out of an order in contempt for not implementing the
judgment and order dated 01.09.2025 passed by the learned Single
Judge of the High Court. After notice was issued in the Contempt
Application and the contemnors were directed to be present in
the Court, Government of U.P. filed a Special Appeal (Defective)
No. 472 of 2026 before the Division Bench of the High Court
against the main judgment and order of the Single Judge dated
29.05.2026. The Division Bench, however, dismissed the Special
Appeal on the ground of delay. The second Appeal arises out of
this order.
3. Heard  Mr.  K.M.  Nataraj,  learned  Additional  Solicitor
General and Mr. Prashant, learned counsel appearing for the
1

## Page 389

respondent(s).
4. Having considered the issues involved in this case and the
circumstances in which the Special Appeal came to be filed, we
are of the opinion that delay in filing the Special Appeal be
condoned. However, this will be subject to costs quantified to
Rs. 50,000/- (Rupees Fifty thousand only), payable to the
respondent(s) within a period of one week from today. 
5. In view of the above, the order dated 29.07.2026 passed by
the Division Bench dismissing the Special Appeal Defective No.
472 of 2026 is set aside and the Special Appeal is restored to
its original number. The Division Bench of the High Court will
hear  the  Special  Appeal  on  merits  and  dispose  it  of  in
accordance with law. 
6. Till the Division Bench decides the Special Appeal, learned
Single Judge may not proceed with the Contempt Application
(Civil) No. 2251 of 2026 and the State shall not take any
coercive action against the respondents towards recoveries.  
7. With these observations, both the Civil Appeals stand
disposed of.

## Page 402

2. This is a case where the Chief Judicial Magistrate,
Udhagamandalam refused to  pass an order under  Section
156(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 directing
registration  of  the  First  Information  Report  (FIR)
against the petitioners.  The High Court, by the impugned
order,  while reversing  the  said  order,  directed
registration of the FIR against the petitioners.
3. Prima facie, it appears to be a matter of a civil
nature.   Learned  senior  counsel  submits  that  the
petitioners, on his own volition, undertakes to deposit
Rs.3,70,00,000/- (Rupees three crores and seventy lakhs).
4. We put it to learned senior counsel for respondent
Nos. 1 and 2 whether his clients are willing to accept
the said amount.
5. Learned senior counsel for respondent Nos. 1 and 2
is very categoric that he has clear instructions not to
accept the  said  amount  and  pursue  the  criminal
proceedings.
6. Leave granted.
7. Since learned senior counsel for the appellants
submits  that  his  clients  are  willing  to  deposit
Rs.3,70,00,000/- (Rupees three crores and seventy lakhs),
we direct the appellants to deposit the aforesaid amount
in this Court within a period of four weeks from today.
2

## Page 403

8. On such deposit, the amount will be kept in a
short-term fixed deposit in any Nationalised bank  on
auto-renewal basis.
9. Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 are at liberty to file an
application to withdraw the said amount.
10. In the meantime, the interim order granted earlier
by this Court on 22 nd August, 2025 shall continue to
operate.
11. In the event, the amount, as voluntarily offered by
the appellants, is not deposited within four weeks, the
interim order granted on 22 nd August, 2025 will stand
vacated.
12. In the event, respondents No. 1 and 2 agree to
withdraw the amount, it is made clear that this Court
would  pass  appropriate  orders  quashing  the  criminal
proceedings.

DEPUTY COMMISSIONER, KENDRIYA VIDYALAYA 
SANGATHAN, BHUBANESWAR REGION & ANR. Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS

(FOR ADMISSION) 
 
Date : 10-08-2026 This petition was called for hearing today.
CORAM : 
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE AHSANUDDIN AMANULLAH
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE R. MAHADEVAN
For Petitioner(s)  Mr. Anil Nag, AoR
                   Ms. Sanya Kashyap, Adv.
                   
                   
For Respondent(s)  Mr. Shibashish Misra, AoR
    Mr. Manav Sabharwal, Adv.
    Ms. Shivangi Gupta, Adv.
    Mr. Nikhil Rajput, Adv.
    Mr. Piyush Negi, Adv.                   
         
                             O R D E R
Heard learned counsels for the parties.
2. The present petition is directed against the impugned order
dated 27.07.2021 passed by the High Court of Orissa at Cuttack in
W.P.(C) No.18587 of 2015 by which, the award dated 07.11.2014
passed in Industrial Dispute Case No.26 of 2007 by the Industrial
Tribunal-Cum-Labour Court holding the termination of the respondent

## Page 456

2
no.1 to be illegal with a direction to the petitioners to reinstate
him in regular payroll with full backwages to be paid within a
period of three months from the date of publication of the award in
the Gazette of India, failing which the petitioners were to pay the
penal interest @12 percentum per annum in cumulative interest, has
been upheld.
3. We have heard the learned counsels for the parties at length.
4. An  initial  plea  was  raised  by  learned  counsel  for  the
petitioners that backwages ought not to have been granted as a
matter of course unless it is justified from the facts and
circumstances of the case.
5. For such proposition, he relied upon a decision of this Court
in the case of Rajasthan State Road Transport Corporation, Jaipur
v. Shri Phool Chand(Dead) Thr. Lrs. (2018) 18 SCC 299.
6. It was further contended by the learned counsel for the
petitioners that the respondent no.1 even otherwise, had not
produced any material before the Court to justify backwages on the
ground that he was not gainfully employed during the period of his
disengagement.
7. Learned counsel for the respondent no.1 submitted that the
respondent no.1 had proved his case of illegal termination on all
counts. It was contended that even with regard to the issue of him
not being employed gainfully, in response to an objection raised by
the petitioners under Section 17B of the Industrial Disputes Act,
1947, the respondent no.1 had taken a categorical stand that he had
not been gainfully employed and such contention has been upheld.
However, to be fair to the Court, it was submitted that since 2022,

## Page 457

3
the  respondent  no.1  was  working  as  a  casual  labourer  in
construction sites and was earning less than Rs.500/- (Rupees Five
Hundred) per day intermittently on the days when he got work. It
was further submitted that the respondent no.1 has been fighting
the litigation without any financial support.
8. Having considered the matter in its entirety, going through
the materials on record and in the background of the facts and
circumstances of this case, we are of the considered view that the
orders of the Courts below do not require any interference.
9. Accordingly,  the  present  Special  Leave  Petition  stands
dismissed.
10. We  not  only  reiterate  the  direction  of  the  Industrial
Tribunal-cum-Labour Court but also direct that payments be made in
terms of the award dated 07.11.2014 passed by the Industrial
Tribunal-cum-Labour Court, latest within a period of three months
from today.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
(SAPNA BISHT)                                   (POOJA KOHLI)
COURT MASTER (SH)                             COURT MASTER (NSH)
